content: The document titled Consolidated Strategic Information Guidelines for Viral Hepatitis: Planning and Tracking Progress Towards Elimination was published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in February 2019. It provides a comprehensive framework for collecting, analyzing, disseminating, and utilizing strategic information on viral hepatitis at local, national, and international levels. The guidelines aim to support countries in achieving the elimination of viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030, as outlined in the Global Health Sector Strategy (GHSS) on viral hepatitis. The GHSS defines elimination as a 90% reduction in new chronic infections and a 65% reduction in mortality compared to 2015 levels. To achieve this, the strategy emphasizes five core interventions: hepatitis B immunization, prevention of mother-to-child transmission of hepatitis B virus (HBV), ensuring blood and injection safety, harm reduction for people who inject drugs, and testing and treatment for hepatitis B and C. These interventions must be implemented at sufficient service coverage levels to meet the 2030 targets. The WHO monitoring and evaluation framework for viral hepatitis B and C adopts a results-based approach, considering the context (e.g., infection prevalence), inputs, outputs, outcomes (including the cascade of prevention, testing, and treatment), and impact (e.g., incidence and mortality). Data systems required to inform this framework include surveillance for acute hepatitis, chronic infections, and sequelae, as well as program data documenting prevention, testing, and treatment efforts. The document highlights the importance of understanding the natural history of HBV and HCV infections, which progress through three phases: new infections (often asymptomatic or presenting as acute hepatitis), chronic infections (usually asymptomatic), and sequelae (cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma) that lead to morbidity and mortality. Surveillance systems must capture all three phases to fully describe the epidemiological situation and guide prevention, testing, and treatment efforts. Surveillance activities include syndromic surveillance in the general population, event-based surveillance, enhanced case reporting with in-vitro diagnostics, regular biomarker surveys, and data triangulation from death certificates and testing of patients with cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma for HBV and HCV. These activities aim to describe the epidemiology of viral hepatitis, including acute and chronic infections and their sequelae. The document also provides standardized case definitions for acute hepatitis surveillance, which can differentiate acute hepatitis from newly diagnosed chronic infections. This information is critical for monitoring trends in acute hepatitis and guiding prevention activities. The guidelines were developed through a collaborative process involving WHO staff, regional offices, and external experts. They were pilot-tested in multiple countries to ensure their relevance and utility for national program managers. The document includes online appendices with template surveillance protocols for acute hepatitis, chronic infections, and sequelae, which received preliminary approval from the WHO Research Ethics Review Committee. In summary, the WHO guidelines provide a strategic framework for countries to collect and use data to inform policy and program decisions, monitor progress, and achieve the elimination of viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030.
